options.label: A step up in cutting feel

all-purpose.title: One everyday knife is enough to start.
all-purpose.why: For general cooking, I start with Victorinox for practical value or Tojiro for a first Japanese gyuto. A 20-21 cm blade handles most board work.
all-purpose.care: Hand-wash and dry after cooking. Use a wood or plastic board and protect the edge in storage.
all-purpose.skip: You can wait on a knife set, a dedicated slicer and high-grit stones.

vegetable.title: Choose a comfortable knife for daily prep.
vegetable.why: A chef's knife already handles onions, herbs and most vegetables well. My starter choices are Victorinox and Tojiro; you do not need to buy a separate nakiri to cook vegetables.
vegetable.care: Keep the board stable. Avoid twisting a thin edge inside hard squash; use a sturdier tool for forceful jobs.
vegetable.skip: A specialised vegetable knife can wait until you know you prefer its flat edge.

small-prep.title: A small, inexpensive paring knife.
small-prep.why: I would keep this simple: a Victorinox Swiss Classic paring knife for peeling, trimming and small fruit. Spending more is optional for this job.
small-prep.care: Choose a straight edge if you want to sharpen it on your normal stone.
small-prep.skip: A premium petty is worth considering later for small tasks on a board.

bread.title: A Victorinox bread knife.
bread.why: A long serrated blade cuts through crust without crushing the loaf. Victorinox is my starting point here, even if you have more to spend.
bread.care: Store the teeth safely. Standard flat-stone sharpening is not the right routine for a serrated edge; consider a specialist service when needed.
bread.skip: No sharpening stone or premium board needs to come with this purchase.

protein.title: A small specialist for trimming.
protein.why: For trimming meat close to bones, I would start with a 15 cm Victorinox boning knife. If you mainly slice boneless portions, the everyday chef's knife you already have may be enough.
protein.care: Cut around bones, not through them. Fish filleting may suit a more flexible blade; match flexibility to the task.
protein.skip: A long Japanese slicer is not necessary for occasional home trimming.

cleaver.title: A thin vegetable slicer, not a bone cleaver.
cleaver.why: For the broad blade and food-scooping shape, look for a light Chinese slicer or cai dao. This is a category search, not a verified model recommendation: check blade thickness, weight and intended use before buying.
cleaver.care: Use for vegetables and boneless food. A tall rectangular blade does not mean it is made to chop bone.
cleaver.skip: If you are unsure about the tall profile, start with a Victorinox chef's knife.

sharpening.title: Start with one 1000-grit stone.
sharpening.why: My first choices are King Deluxe 1000 for a lower-cost start and Shapton Kuromaku / Pro 1000 for less preparation. Learn to make a consistent edge before adding finer stones.
sharpening.care: Follow the exact stone's wetting and drying instructions. Keep it stable in use and flatten it as it wears.
sharpening.skip: You do not need a 6000-grit stone or a strop to begin. A flattening method will become useful.

board.title: A stable board with room to work.
board.why: I would start with a generously sized food-grade polyethylene board that fits your sink. If you want to spend more on cutting feel, an Asahi rubber board is an optional step up.
board.care: Prevent slipping and clean according to the maker's directions. Check dimensions and whether the particular board is dishwasher-safe.
board.skip: Glass, stone and ceramic cutting surfaces are poor companions for a fine knife edge.

storage.title: Protect the edge you already have.
storage.why: A correctly sized blade guard is a simple starting point for drawer storage. There is no need to buy a full knife block.
storage.care: Measure blade height and length before ordering. Put the knife away clean and completely dry.
storage.skip: A knife roll is only useful if you regularly transport your knives.
